title: Monomial differences in an ideal define a congruence
statement:
Let $M$ be a commutative monoid written additively, let $A$ be a commutative ring, and write $A[M]$ for the free $A$-module [def-weil-pbc-free-module] with basis $[m]$, $m\in M$, and multiplication $[u][v]=[u+v]$, extended $A$-bilinearly, with unit $[0]$. Let $J$ be any ideal of $A[M]$, meaning an additive subgroup stable under multiplication by arbitrary elements of $A[M]$. Define $d_J(u,v)$ to mean $[u]-[v]\in J$. Then $d_J$ is a monoid congruence: it is an equivalence relation and $d_J(u,v)$ implies $d_J(u+w,v+w)$ for every $w\in M$. Let $S\subseteq M\times M$ be any set, and let $c$ be the smallest monoid congruence containing $S$, namely the intersection of all equivalence relations preserved by addition and containing $S$. Then
$$c\subseteq d_J\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad [u]-[v]\in J\text{ for every }(u,v)\in S.$$
In particular, whenever $J$ contains those generating differences, it contains $[u]-[v]$ for every pair with $c(u,v)$. No finiteness of $S$, cancellation in $M$, or properness of $J$ is assumed.

proof.text: The additive-subgroup condition on $J$ gives $0\in J$ and closure under negation and addition. Thus $[u]-[u]=0\in J$; if $[u]-[v]\in J$, then $[v]-[u]=-([u]-[v])\in J$; and if $[u]-[v]\in J$ and $[v]-[t]\in J$, then $[u]-[t]=([u]-[v])+([v]-[t])\in J$. These three calculations prove reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity of $d_J$.

proof.text: If $d_J(u,v)$ and $w\in M$, ideal closure gives $([u]-[v])[w]\in J$. The specified bilinear multiplication gives $([u]-[v])[w]=[u+w]-[v+w]$, hence $d_J(u+w,v+w)$. Together with step 1 this proves the required monoid congruence. It also gives the two-variable compatibility if desired: from $d_J(u,v)$ and $d_J(w,z)$, translation gives $d_J(u+w,v+w)$ and $d_J(w+v,z+v)$; commutativity and transitivity give $d_J(u+w,v+z)$.

source.place: Agent calculation from ideal closure and the multiplication law in the item; comparison with AddCon compatibility.

proof.text: Let $\mathcal C$ be the family of monoid congruences containing $S$. This family is nonempty since the universal relation belongs to it. By the stated definition, $c(u,v)$ means $r(u,v)$ for every $r\in\mathcal C$. Every pair in $S$ belongs to every such $r$, hence to $c$. Consequently $c\subseteq d_J$ implies that every $S$-difference lies in $J$. Conversely, if every $S$-difference lies in $J$, then $S\subseteq d_J$; steps 1 and 2 show $d_J\in\mathcal C$. Evaluating the intersection at this member gives $c\subseteq d_J$. Unfolding $d_J$ yields the claimed propagation of all $c$-related differences. No step uses finiteness, cancellation, or properness.
